# Summary

**Data source overview.** Martínez-Plumed et al. (IJCAI-18) propose nine "facets" (each with several "edges") for characterising the object of AI (functionality, referent, generality, location, embodiment) and AI as a discipline (paradigm, actor, character, nature). They validate the framework quantitatively with keyword/tag mappings over 20 years of AAAI/IJCAI proceedings (DBLP) and ~50 years of the AAAI *AI topics* archive, and then use the facets qualitatively to argue for a non-anthropocentric "intelligence landscape", ability-oriented characterisation of AI, and compensatory governance actions against dominant-paradigm bias.

**EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[72]**
The paper is a meta-scientific/bibliometric framework paper, not an AI-safety technical paper, so risks and interventions are largely *implicit* (definitional instability hindering regulation, winner-takes-all paradigm bias, weakening of scientific/philosophical framing making safety and governance harder, anthropocentric evaluation blind spots, attribution problems in hybrid human-AI systems). Moderate inference was therefore needed to convert the paper's descriptive claims into safety-relevant risk → intervention pathways. *Instruction improvements that would help*: (i) explicit guidance for meta-scientific / bibliometric / field-mapping sources where "risk" is about the epistemic health and governability of the field rather than model behaviour; (ii) an allowed edge verb set for "theoretical insight → design rationale" and "mechanism → intervention" transitions (currently only "motivates" from validation evidence is specified, forcing awkward routings); (iii) explicit direction convention (source = earlier node in causal flow) to remove ambiguity in passive-voice verbs like `caused_by`; (iv) a rule for how to treat framework *dimensions* (facets) — whether each facet is one mechanism node or several.

**Inference strategy justification.** Risk nodes were derived from statements the authors make explicitly about consequences ("policy makers ... wrestle with the problem of defining what systems are actually AI"; "bias towards reinforcing the dominant view ... the winner takes all"; "concern in AI safety and governance, usually harder to handle when the engineering and scientific perspectives are weak"; "harder to differentiate how performance can be attributed realistically"; "we do not want to replicate certain behaviours humans display (e.g., gender bias)"). Interventions were derived from the authors' own recommendations (apply the framework, use the published data/code/Shiny app, compensatory actions for less popular areas, academia/government prioritisation, ability-oriented evaluation, universal landscape reference, contribution tracing), plus two lightly inferred safety interventions (regulatory scope definition; bias screening), marked with confidence 1–2.

**Extraction completeness.** All nine facets are decomposed into white-box component mechanism nodes (functionality/referent/generality-location-embodiment/paradigm-actor-character-nature), the two data pipelines (DBLP keyword mapping, AI topics substring tagging) are separate mechanisms, and all reported empirical results (ML rise, KR/heuristic-search decline, peaks/cycles, cross-source consistency, security-privacy-safety rise, facet share shifts, flat universal edge) are validation-evidence nodes feeding interventions.

**Key limitations.** Edge confidences are mostly 2–3: the evidence is descriptive bibliometrics on two non-exhaustive corpora (no ECAI/ICML/NIPS), with keyword-mapping subjectivity and no statistical hypothesis testing; the authors themselves warn the trends must not be used for forecasting. The safety framing is largely inferred by the extractor.
